messages.content: I want to design a software-defined routing system that supports concurrent, overlapping route updates. Every packet must follow one committed routing configuration, even if updates overlap or the controller crashes. I also need peak per-switch rules limited to 2× max(initial, final), and updates must complete after controller connectivity recovers.

That sets three requirements for the design. It must allow route updates to be in progress concurrently even when they overlap; it must preserve per-packet consistency through those updates and controller crashes; and it must respect the per-switch rule limit while still completing updates after connectivity recovers. The requirements describe what the system must guarantee, rather than prescribing a particular update mechanism.
Can you unpack “one committed routing configuration” for a packet?

The packet must be handled according to a single committed configuration throughout its route. It must not encounter a mixture of routing decisions that, taken together, belong only to an unfinished update. The configuration need not be the same one followed by every other packet; the requirement is consistency for each packet individually.
So two packets in flight at the same time could follow different configurations?

Yes, provided each packet follows one configuration that has been committed. Per-packet consistency does not require all packets in flight to switch configurations at the same instant. It rules out an individual packet receiving an inconsistent combination of decisions while the routing state changes.
Does it matter that the route updates overlap, rather than merely happening at the same time?

Yes. The design cannot rely on concurrent updates affecting entirely separate routing state. Their effects may intersect, yet packets still have to follow committed configurations, and the rule limit still has to hold. The requirement does not specify how the system orders or coordinates those intersecting updates.
Does supporting concurrent updates mean their effects must become committed simultaneously?

Not necessarily. Concurrent updates can be in progress at the same time without a requirement that they commit at exactly the same time. What matters here is that the system supports the overlap and that each packet follows one committed configuration despite it. No particular commit order is stated.
What changes if the controller crashes while those updates are underway?

The crash must not undermine the packet-level guarantee. A packet cannot be made to follow an uncommitted mixture of routing decisions merely because the controller stopped during an update. The design also has to allow the updates to complete after controller connectivity recovers; the requirement does not say they must finish while that connectivity is unavailable.
Is recovery just a safety requirement, or is there a progress requirement too?

There is both. Every packet following one committed configuration is the safety requirement, including during overlapping updates and controller crashes. Completing updates after controller connectivity recovers is the progress requirement. Preserving consistency alone would not satisfy the stated goal if interrupted updates could never complete after recovery.
Does “after connectivity recovers” impose a specific completion time?

No time limit is given. The stated condition is that updates complete after controller connectivity recovers. It does not provide a deadline or claim that completion occurs during a period when connectivity has not recovered.
How should I read the 2× max(initial, final) limit?

It is a peak rule-count limit for each switch. If I and F are that switch’s rule counts in the initial and final configurations, and P is its peak rule count during the update, the stated bound is P ≤ 2 × max(I, F). It is based on the larger of the initial and final counts, not on their sum and not on a network-wide average.
Does the bound apply only once the updates are finished?

No. “Peak” concerns the maximum number of rules present at a switch during the update, including any temporary increase associated with changing configurations. A low final rule count would not, by itself, establish that the peak stayed within the limit.
Could overlapping updates each use their own allowance and exceed the limit together?

The requirement is phrased as a limit on peak per-switch rules, without an exception for overlap. Concurrent work therefore cannot be treated as exempt from that limit. Where multiple updates overlap, the design must account for their combined effect on the rules present at a switch while applying the stated initial–final bound.
Is this a bound on the total number of rules across all switches?

No. It is explicitly per switch. Keeping the network-wide total low would not make up for an individual switch exceeding its allowed peak. Conversely, the statement does not specify a separate limit on the sum across switches.
If packets stay consistent, does that automatically keep the rule count within the bound?

No. They are separate requirements. An update process could preserve a committed configuration for every packet yet use too many rules at a switch. It could also stay within the rule limit without ensuring that every packet follows one committed configuration. A satisfactory design needs both properties, as well as completion after connectivity recovers.
Does per-packet consistency also promise that no packets are dropped?

That is not stated as a separate guarantee. The specified requirement is that every packet follows one committed routing configuration despite overlapping updates and controller crashes. It would be an addition to claim a broader guarantee about every possible cause of packet loss or other data-plane behavior.
Then the central challenge is handling packets and unfinished updates without treating a crash as permission to expose partial routing state?

Exactly. Overlap and crashes are conditions under which the guarantees must continue to hold, not exceptions to them. The design has to keep each packet within one committed routing configuration, keep each switch’s peak rules at or below 2× max(initial, final), and complete updates once controller connectivity recovers.

For the design, I propose serializing overlapping updates and using durable epochs, dual rule banks, ingress tags, drain acknowledgments, and 2× endpoint-rule admission. How do those pieces fit together?

They form a proposed way to separate three concerns. Serializing overlapping updates addresses interference between changes to the same routing state. Durable epochs give an update an identity that can survive a controller crash. Dual rule banks and ingress tags are meant to let packets be handled according to a selected configuration while old and new rules coexist; drain acknowledgments address when rules for older packets can be removed. The 2× endpoint-rule admission check addresses the peak per-switch rule limit. These are design elements, not by themselves a proof that every requirement is met.
Does serializing overlapping updates conflict with the goal of supporting concurrent updates?

Not necessarily. The proposal is to serialize updates that overlap, rather than require all update requests to arrive one at a time. Concurrent requests can exist while conflicting changes are coordinated in an order. The proposal does not, on its own, specify whether nonoverlapping updates proceed in parallel or exactly how overlap is detected.
Why identify updates with durable epochs?

An epoch can distinguish one routing configuration or update stage from another, so a packet’s selected rules can be associated with the intended committed configuration. Making the epoch durable is relevant to controller crashes: after connectivity recovers, recovery should not have to infer the update’s identity solely from a controller’s lost working memory. The proposal does not yet specify what records are durable or how their contents are reconciled with switch state.
What is the point of two rule banks?

The dual-bank idea is to keep rules associated with the existing configuration available while rules for another configuration are present. That coexistence can support a transition without forcing an in-flight packet to encounter rules from an unintended mixture. Two banks alone do not establish per-packet consistency: the way packets select a bank, the meaning of an epoch, and the conditions for reclaiming rules also matter.
Is that where ingress tags come in?

Yes, conceptually. An ingress tag can mark which committed configuration a packet should follow, so forwarding decisions can select rules associated with that configuration as the packet proceeds. The important property is that the packet’s association does not change midway merely because an overlapping update is underway. The proposal does not specify a tag format or a particular switch implementation.
Would installing rules in the other bank itself make the new configuration committed?

Not just by virtue of installing them. Having rules present and deciding that packets may use a committed configuration are distinct concepts. If packets could encounter partially prepared rules as though they were a committed configuration, dual banks and tags would not deliver the intended guarantee. The proposal needs a clear distinction between preparation and what ingress tags are permitted to select, though it does not yet state a specific commit procedure.
What do drain acknowledgments contribute after a change?

They are meant to provide a basis for knowing when packets associated with an older configuration no longer need its rules. Removing those rules too early could strand a packet that was already tagged for the older committed configuration. A drain acknowledgment is therefore relevant to safe rule reclamation; the proposal has not specified who issues one, how its scope is determined, or what evidence makes it trustworthy.
So the old bank is not simply cleared as soon as new packets use a different tag?

Right. New packets being associated with another configuration does not, by itself, establish that no previously tagged packets remain. The drain-acknowledgment component is intended to distinguish a change in how new packets are handled from the point at which old rules are no longer needed by packets already in flight.
How does 2× endpoint-rule admission fit with keeping two banks?

The admission component is intended to check rule capacity before an update proceeds, accounting for rules that may coexist. The target remains the stated peak per-switch limit: 2× max(initial, final), using that switch’s endpoint rule counts. The existence of two banks does not automatically prove the bound, especially with overlapping requests or rules that remain present while packets drain. Admission has to consider the actual peak that the proposed work could require at each affected switch.
Does “2× endpoint-rule admission” mean counting only the final rules?

No. The comparison is to twice the larger of the initial and final per-switch rule counts, and the quantity being constrained is the peak during the update. An admission decision focused only on the final count would miss temporary coexistence. Calling it endpoint-rule admission identifies the counts used for the bound; it does not remove the need to account for temporary rules when applying it.
If overlapping updates are serialized, can their rule footprints still matter at the same time?

Potentially, which is why the serialization proposal should not be mistaken for a complete resource argument. Ordering overlapping updates is about which changes may proceed against intersecting state. Rules needed by packets from a prior committed configuration may still be present while those packets drain. The admission check must address what is actually resident at a switch, rather than assuming an ordering decision has already freed the capacity.
How would these elements relate to a crash in the middle of an update?

The proposed roles are complementary: durable epochs provide persistent identity for recovery, while tags and banks are intended to keep packet handling tied to committed configurations even when the controller is unavailable. Drain acknowledgments matter when deciding whether old rules can safely be reclaimed. To meet the goal, the recovered controller would still need to complete updates after connectivity recovers. The proposal names the relevant mechanisms but does not yet define a full crash-recovery protocol or establish that it always makes progress.
Could recovery just assume that whichever bank looks newer is committed?

That assumption would need justification that the proposal has not supplied. A bank can contain rules without those rules necessarily constituting a committed configuration for packets. The durable epoch and the distinction between installed rules and committed packet behavior are particularly important when reasoning about recovery from an interrupted update.
What should I avoid claiming about this proposal at this stage?

Avoid claiming that the named components alone prove per-packet consistency, crash recovery, or the 2× bound. They describe a plausible division of responsibilities: coordinate overlapping updates, retain recoverable update identity, keep configuration-specific rules available, associate packets with a committed configuration, wait for old packets to drain, and admit work subject to the per-switch peak limit. The exact coordination, acknowledgment semantics, and resource accounting remain to be specified before those guarantees can be established.
How can recovery determine which ingress epoch was activated before a controller crash without exposing packets to mixed routes?

The key distinction is between an epoch being known to the controller and that epoch actually being activated at ingress. After a crash, recovery needs trustworthy evidence of what ingress could have selected before it decides how to proceed. Knowing that rules for an epoch were prepared, or that the epoch was recorded durably, does not by itself establish that packets were admitted under its tag.
Why is the activation point so important?

Ingress activation affects which committed configuration a packet is associated with when it enters. If recovery guesses incorrectly, it could treat an epoch as unused when packets already carry its tag, or treat a prepared epoch as though it had been activated. Either mistake complicates preserving the requirement that each packet follow one committed configuration. The question is therefore about determining what packets could actually have been told to follow, not merely what update the controller intended.
Suppose the crash happens right around activation. Is that the ambiguous case?

Yes. The controller might have initiated a change without knowing, after it recovers, whether activation took effect before the crash. That is the uncertainty recovery must resolve or safely accommodate. The question does not supply an activation or acknowledgment protocol, so it does not yet establish which evidence would settle that case.
Would the durable epoch alone settle it?

Not necessarily. Durability can preserve an epoch’s identity across a crash, but the fact that an epoch exists is different from evidence that ingress activated it. Recovery would need to connect any durable information it relies on to the actual activation state. Otherwise it risks confusing an intended transition with one that packets may already be using.
Could recovery simply pick the older epoch to be safe?

Picking an epoch without establishing what happened at ingress is not enough. Packets admitted before the crash may already be associated with another committed epoch. Recovery has to preserve valid handling for packets that could be in flight while it determines how ingress should behave going forward. The question leaves open how that determination is made.
Does the same problem arise if recovery assumes the newer epoch was activated?

Yes. Rules being present for a newer epoch do not alone show that ingress began selecting it, or that it was committed for packet use. Recovery should not infer activation solely from preparation. The issue is not whether older or newer sounds safer; it is whether the conclusion reflects an activation state that can be established without exposing a packet to mixed routes.
What does “without exposing packets to mixed routes” require during that investigation?

As recovery determines what occurred, each packet still needs routing decisions belonging to one committed configuration. Uncertainty about which ingress epoch was activated cannot be passed on to packets as a mixture of rules from different configurations. In particular, recovery cannot safely reclaim rules needed by packets of a possibly active epoch merely because the controller has not yet confirmed that activation occurred.
How do ingress tags and the two rule banks relate to the question?

Ingress tags are intended to associate packets with a configuration, and dual rule banks are intended to keep configuration-specific rules available through a transition. Together they provide a way to think about consistent packet handling while an activation question is resolved. But neither component, just by existing, tells a recovered controller which epoch ingress actually activated before the crash.
Is this mainly a question about packets that entered before the crash, or packets that enter after connectivity returns?

Both matter, in different ways. Packets already admitted may need the rules for the epoch under which they entered. For later packets, recovery must know what ingress is selecting or ensure that its subsequent actions do not create an inconsistent selection. The common concern is that uncertainty about pre-crash activation must not cause either group to encounter mixed routes.
Would a drain acknowledgment answer which epoch had been activated?

Its proposed purpose is different: a drain acknowledgment concerns when packets needing an older configuration’s rules have ceased to require them. That could matter for safe cleanup, but it is not automatically evidence of which ingress epoch was activated at the crash boundary. Whether it supplies useful evidence would depend on acknowledgment semantics that have not been specified.
So what, exactly, must a recovery design establish?

It must establish, or safely account for uncertainty about, which ingress epoch could have been selected before the crash. It must keep the rules needed by packets admitted under committed configurations available while doing so, and avoid directing packets into a partially prepared or mixed configuration. The question identifies that recovery obligation; it does not yet choose a particular way to record or verify activation.
Is the question asking whether the update completed before the crash?

More narrowly, it asks which ingress epoch was activated before the crash and how recovery can determine that without compromising packet consistency. Completion of the broader update is a separate issue: even once activation is understood, there may still be packets using an earlier configuration and update work to finish after controller connectivity recovers.

Here is a hypothesis for the recovery question: a durable commit before ingress flips, followed by per-ingress epoch queries on restart, prevents mixed-version paths across 1,000 controller-crash injections.

That is a specific hypothesis, not yet an observed result. It proposes an ordering rule—make the commit durable before allowing ingress epochs to flip—and a recovery check—query each ingress for its epoch when the controller restarts. The proposed outcome is that packets do not encounter mixed-version paths across 1,000 controller-crash injections.
Why does the durable commit need to come before the ingress flips?

If an ingress can select the new epoch, packets may enter under that epoch. Placing the durable commit first is intended to ensure that recovery can recognize that configuration as committed even if the controller crashes after an ingress flips. The ordering addresses the gap between what ingress may actually select and what the restarted controller can establish from durable state.
Would the durable commit tell recovery that every ingress flipped?

No. It would establish the proposed commit ordering, not that every ingress acted on a flip. That is why the hypothesis also calls for per-ingress epoch queries on restart: recovery needs to distinguish ingresses that activated the epoch from those that did not, rather than treating a durable commit as proof of uniform activation.
So different ingresses might report different epochs after the same crash?

They might. A crash could interrupt the sequence of ingress flips, and the hypothesis explicitly calls for querying each ingress rather than assuming they all have the same state. Different reported epochs would not, by themselves, prove that an individual packet followed a mixed-version path. The packet-level question is whether a packet entering under a given epoch continues to use the corresponding committed routing configuration.
How does querying on restart help with the uncertainty we discussed?

It asks each ingress what epoch it actually has after the crash, instead of inferring activation from the controller’s intention to flip it. Paired with a commit that precedes flips, those answers are proposed to give recovery a basis for reasoning about which committed epochs ingress could have selected. The hypothesis still needs validation that the queried state is an adequate account of activation relevant to packets.
What if the controller crashes before the durable commit?

Under the proposed ordering, no ingress flip for that commit should have occurred yet. That is the intended safety significance of putting the durable commit first. Whether an implementation actually preserves that ordering at every ingress is part of what would need to be checked; the hypothesis alone does not demonstrate it.
And if it crashes after the commit but before all the flips?

The commit is durable, while the ingresses may be in different epoch states. On restart, per-ingress queries are intended to expose that difference so recovery does not guess which flips occurred. The proposed consistency argument depends on packets from each ingress retaining routing behavior associated with their selected committed epoch, rather than being sent through a mixture because activation was only partial.
Does the hypothesis require all ingresses to flip atomically?

No atomic, simultaneous flip is stated. In fact, per-ingress queries are relevant precisely because the ingresses might not all have flipped before a crash. The hypothesis concerns preventing mixed-version paths for packets despite that uncertainty; it does not claim that all ingresses always display the same epoch at a given moment.
What is meant by “mixed-version paths” here?

It refers to a packet encountering routing decisions from different configurations along its path, rather than following one committed configuration throughout. Seeing packets associated with different committed epochs at the same time is not necessarily a mixed-version path. The problematic case is a single packet receiving an inconsistent combination of versions.
Does the number 1,000 mean this has already been demonstrated?

No. The statement is a hypothesis about what would happen across 1,000 controller-crash injections. It specifies the number of injections in the proposed check, but supplies no results from running them. We should not describe the absence of mixed-version paths as an established experimental finding.
Should I read it as 1,000 crashes at one particular point in an update?

The hypothesis specifies 1,000 controller-crash injections, but it does not specify their timing or distribution. It would be unwarranted to assign them all to one point, or to claim they cover every possible point. The stated outcome to examine is whether any injected crash exposes a packet to a mixed-version path.
If queries come back with different epochs, would that automatically refute the hypothesis?

No. Different ingress epochs can reflect an interrupted set of flips without showing that any packet took a mixed-version path. A refutation of the proposed outcome would require evidence of that packet-level inconsistency under the crashes being examined. The per-ingress differences are information recovery must handle, not inherently a violation.
Could the controller rely only on the ingress queries, without the durable commit?

That would be a different claim. The stated hypothesis combines durable commit before ingress flips with queries on restart. The queries address which epochs were activated at individual ingresses; the durable commit addresses whether an epoch that ingress could select had already been committed. Neither role should be silently dropped when evaluating this particular hypothesis.
And a durable commit alone would leave the activation question open?

Yes. Committing before flips helps ensure that a flipped epoch corresponds to a committed configuration, but the commit record alone does not identify which individual ingresses flipped before the crash. The proposed queries address that remaining uncertainty.
Is the 2× max(initial, final) rule bound part of what this hypothesis establishes?

No. This hypothesis is about crash recovery and preventing mixed-version paths through commit ordering and per-ingress queries. The per-switch peak rule limit remains a separate design requirement; no rule-count measurements or proof of that bound are included in this hypothesis.
What would be a careful way to state the claim while it remains untested?

You could say: “We hypothesize that committing durably before any ingress epoch flip, then querying each ingress’s epoch after controller restart, prevents mixed-version packet paths across 1,000 controller-crash injections.” That preserves the proposed mechanism, the specific count, and the intended outcome without presenting the outcome as a completed result.

I want to turn the recovery idea into a plan: journal the prepared rule banks and the commit, flip ingress epochs, then, after injected controller crashes, reconcile queried tags before draining old rules.

That gives the plan a clear sequence: record the prepared banks and commit, perform the ingress flips, and use queried ingress tags to reconcile what happened after an injected crash. Draining old rules comes only after that reconciliation. This is a proposed procedure, not a report that it has been executed or that it has prevented mixed routes.
Why journal the prepared banks as well as the commit?

They represent different information. The prepared-bank record concerns which configuration-specific rules were prepared; the commit record concerns which configuration was committed. Keeping both in the plan lets recovery distinguish preparation from commitment rather than assuming that the presence of prepared rules means packets were authorized to use them. The plan does not specify the journal’s format or exactly what it records for each bank.
Does journaling a prepared bank mean ingress has already begun using it?

No. Preparation and ingress activation are separate steps in this plan. A journaled prepared bank does not, by itself, say that an ingress flipped its epoch or that packets entered under that epoch. That is why the later queries matter.
How important is the order between the commit and the ingress flips?

It is central to the stated sequence: the commit is journaled before ingress epochs are flipped. The intended distinction is that ingress activation follows a recorded commit, rather than turning a prepared configuration into something packets might use before its commit is recorded. Whether a particular implementation enforces that order is not established by stating the plan.
What would the queried tags tell us after a crash?

They are intended to show the ingress epoch state observed after the crash. Recovery can compare those observations with the journaled preparation and commit instead of assuming that every planned flip either occurred or failed. The plan says to reconcile the queried tags; it does not yet define the query’s precise guarantees or a rule for resolving every possible observation.
Why query rather than just resume the next step in the journal?

A journal can record the intended sequence and its committed state, but an injected crash might occur while ingress flips are underway. Simply advancing from the journal could mistake an intended flip for an activated one, or overlook a flip that took effect. Reconciling queried tags addresses that uncertainty before recovery acts on assumptions about which epochs packets may have used.
If some queried tags show one epoch and others show another, is that necessarily a failure?

Not necessarily. It may indicate that the crash interrupted the ingress flips. The plan calls for reconciling the reported states, not for treating differing tags alone as proof that a packet followed mixed routes. The packet-level concern is whether each packet continues to follow one committed routing configuration.
Why place reconciliation before draining old rules?

Old rules might still be needed by packets admitted under an earlier epoch. Until recovery has accounted for which ingress tags could have been used, draining those rules could remove forwarding behavior that such packets need. The plan therefore places reconciliation first; it does not claim that reconciliation alone proves all older packets have drained.
So reconciliation and draining answer different questions?

Yes. Reconciliation addresses what the queried ingress states mean in light of the journaled banks and commit after a crash. Draining concerns when old rules are no longer needed by packets using the older configuration. The sequence keeps the first question from being skipped when deciding whether to proceed with the second.
Does the plan say how a drain acknowledgment is produced?

No. Drain acknowledgments are part of the proposed design context, but this plan only says to reconcile queried tags before draining old rules. It does not specify who acknowledges a drain, what the acknowledgment covers, or how recovery verifies it.
Where do the injected crashes enter the sequence?

They interrupt the planned update so the recovery path can be examined. After an injected crash, the plan calls for querying tags and reconciling the answers against the journal before old rules are drained. It does not state the number of injections, their timing, or any results.
Should I describe this as having demonstrated that packets never take mixed-version paths?

No. The node is a plan for how to record, activate, and recover around injected crashes. Preventing mixed-version paths is the consistency property the plan is meant to address, but no execution results or proof are stated here.
And does this plan by itself settle the per-switch 2× max(initial, final) bound?

No. Journaling, ingress flips, tag reconciliation, and draining describe an update and recovery sequence. They do not, by themselves, establish the peak rule count at each switch. The per-switch bound remains a separate requirement to account for when prepared and old rules coexist.
Can you state the recovery plan without implying a particular answer to an ambiguous query?

Journal the prepared banks and the commit before flipping ingress epochs. Following an injected controller crash, query the ingress tags and reconcile the observed states with those journaled records before draining old rules. That states the intended ordering and recovery check without presuming what any ingress will report or claiming the check has already succeeded.
Let’s run CrashEpoch-1K: inject 1,000 controller crashes around commits and ingress flips, then count mixed-version packet paths after restart reconciliation.

CrashEpoch-1K is a concrete activity for examining the recovery behavior. The specified work is to inject 1,000 crashes around commits and ingress flips and count mixed-version packet paths after restart reconciliation. That describes what to run and measure; it does not report a count or say the activity has already succeeded.
What makes commits and ingress flips the relevant places for the crashes?

They bracket the uncertainty this activity is meant to examine. A commit concerns whether a configuration has been committed, while an ingress flip concerns which epoch packets may actually enter under. A crash around either event can leave the restarting controller needing to reconcile what was committed with what ingress activated. The activity does not specify exact injection points or their distribution among those events.
Is CrashEpoch-1K a test of the idea that committing before ingress flips and querying epochs on restart prevents mixed-version paths?

Yes. It is an activity aimed at evaluating that proposed recovery behavior under injected crashes. Its observable outcome is the count of mixed-version packet paths after restart reconciliation. The proposal and the test activity should still be distinguished from a result: no observed count has been supplied.
When you say “after restart reconciliation,” what part of the sequence are we measuring?

The count is tied to packet paths in the recovery setting after the restarted controller reconciles ingress-epoch information. That condition matters because the activity is not merely checking whether the controller can restart; it is checking whether packet paths remain version-consistent when recovery has to account for the state left by a crash. The activity does not specify a narrower observation window or a particular counting procedure.
Could I just count how many ingresses report the newer epoch?

That would answer a different question. Ingress-epoch information is relevant to reconciliation, but the stated measurement is the number of mixed-version packet paths. Different ingresses reporting different epochs would not, by itself, show that any single packet followed a path combining versions.
Then what should count as one mixed-version packet path?

Conceptually, it is a path on which an individual packet receives routing decisions from different versions rather than following one committed routing configuration. The unit of concern is the packet’s path, not the number of epoch values reported by ingresses or the number of configurations present in the system. CrashEpoch-1K names that outcome to count without specifying an instrumentation method.
Does “1,000” refer to crashes, packet paths, or restarts?

It refers to 1,000 injected crashes. The number of mixed-version packet paths is the outcome to count; the activity does not prescribe that outcome in advance. It also does not state how many packet paths will be observed in connection with those crash injections.
Are the 1,000 crashes all supposed to happen at exactly the commit boundary?

No such restriction is stated. The activity says to inject them around commits and ingress flips. It does not assign a count to either kind of event or define exact timing relative to each one, so we should not turn “around” into a more specific schedule.
Why count paths after reconciliation instead of treating a successful restart as enough?

A controller returning after a crash does not, on its own, show that packets avoided mixed-version routes. Reconciliation is meant to address uncertainty about ingress epochs, and the path count examines the packet-level consequence in that recovery setting. The stated activity focuses on consistency, not merely on whether the controller becomes available again.
If the count is zero, what would I be entitled to say?

If zero were actually observed, you could report that no mixed-version packet paths were counted in CrashEpoch-1K’s 1,000 injected-crash runs under its observation conditions. That would be an experimental result for those injections, not a proof covering every possible crash timing or system execution. At present, no zero count—or any other count—has been reported.
And if a mixed-version path is counted?

That would be an observed packet-level inconsistency in the activity, rather than merely an ingress-epoch difference. The count would establish that the proposed outcome did not hold for all observed paths in those runs. The activity statement alone would not identify which part of commit, flip, or reconciliation behavior caused it.
Can the test tell us whether the 2× max(initial, final) per-switch rule limit holds?

Not from the stated measurement. CrashEpoch-1K counts mixed-version packet paths after restart reconciliation; it does not call for measuring peak rules at each switch. The 2× max(initial, final) limit remains a separate requirement and cannot be inferred from a path count.
Does it establish that updates complete after controller connectivity recovers?

Not by itself. The activity explicitly involves restart reconciliation and a count of mixed-version paths, but it does not specify a completion measurement. An observed path count would address the stated consistency outcome under crash injections, not automatically establish update completion after connectivity recovers.
Should we describe the restart reconciliation as already having worked?

No. Here it is part of the activity’s recovery sequence, not a reported success. The wording can say that CrashEpoch-1K injects crashes around commits and ingress flips and counts mixed-version packet paths after restart reconciliation, without asserting what reconciliation will reveal or whether the resulting count will be zero.
So what is the most precise one-sentence description of CrashEpoch-1K at this point?
CrashEpoch-1K is an activity to inject 1,000 controller crashes around commits and ingress flips and count mixed-version packet paths after restart reconciliation; no results are stated.
CrashEpoch-1K observed zero mixed-version packet paths across 1,000 crashes. Restart queries also reconciled every ingress epoch.

Those are the observed results: the mixed-version packet-path count was zero across the 1,000 injected crashes, and the restart queries reconciled every ingress epoch. The result is specific to what CrashEpoch-1K observed; it is not a claim about every possible crash or execution.
What exactly does the zero count say about packets?

It says that no packet path observed in CrashEpoch-1K was counted as combining routing versions. It is a packet-path observation, not a statement that all ingresses necessarily displayed the same epoch at every moment.
And what does “reconciled every ingress epoch” add?

It says that the restart queries accounted for the epoch at every ingress in these runs. That matters to the recovery question because the controller needed to determine ingress epoch state after a crash, rather than infer it solely from the fact that a commit or flip had been initiated. The result does not give the individual epoch values returned by those queries.
Can I say every ingress had flipped before each crash?
No. Reconciling every ingress epoch means the queried epochs were accounted for; it does not say they were all the same, or that every ingress had flipped before any particular crash.
Could some ingresses have had different epochs without producing a mixed-version packet path?

Conceptually, yes: different packets can follow different committed configurations without an individual packet encountering a mixture. But the reported evidence does not specify whether differing ingress epochs were observed. It reports that every ingress epoch was reconciled and that the mixed-version packet-path count was zero.
Does the result tell us which side of a commit or flip each crash landed on?

No. The activity placed crashes around commits and ingress flips, but this result does not break down crash timing or report the queried state for individual injections. We should not infer a particular distribution of crash points from the aggregate count of 1,000.
Is “zero across 1,000 crashes” the same as saying every possible packet path was checked?

Is it accurate to say the observed mixed-version paths were eliminated in the rerun?

Should we mention the drain acknowledgments when describing the result?

No. The observation is about mixed-version packet paths, not universal agreement among ingress tags at every instant. It does not report the ingress-tag values during the trials.
What if someone interprets “all trials completed” as meaning no packet was dropped?

That would be an unsupported interpretation. Trial completion after reconnection and the absence of observed mixed-version paths do not provide a packet-loss measurement. Neither reported outcome states whether packets were dropped.
Is the result enough to say every possible overlapping update will complete after any crash?
No. It reports completion in all 1,000 crash trials of this OverlapCrash-1K rerun after reconnection. It does not cover every possible overlapping-update pattern, crash, or execution.
And what about the 2× max(initial, final) peak per-switch rule bound?

This evidence does not report peak per-switch rule counts. Zero mixed-version paths and completion after reconnection address consistency and progress in the rerun, but they do not establish the separate 2× max(initial, final) rule bound.
What is the most careful concise statement of the result?
With epoch-tag reservations, OverlapCrash-1K recorded zero mixed-version paths versus 14 previously, and all 1,000 crash trials completed after reconnection.
Can dual rule banks stay within 2× max(initial, final) when serialized overlapping updates create larger intermediate configurations?

Not automatically. Serialization can control which overlapping update proceeds, but it does not by itself limit the size of an intermediate configuration. Dual banks may temporarily hold rules for two configurations, so their combined per-switch occupancy must be checked against 2× max(initial, final), using the stated initial and final rule counts. A sufficiently large intermediate configuration could make that bound impossible to meet, even before accounting for a second bank.
Is the concern that each bank could be as large as the final configuration?

The concern is broader. One or both resident banks might represent an intermediate configuration whose per-switch rule count exceeds the larger endpoint count. Assuming that two banks each fit within max(initial, final) would miss that possibility. What matters for the bound is the peak number of rules actually present at each switch.
Could you state the comparison with symbols?

For a given switch, let I and F be its rule counts in the initial and final configurations, and let B = max(I, F). The required peak limit is P ≤ 2B, where P is the largest number of rules present at that switch during the update. If two banks concurrently contain A and C rules at that switch, their combined occupancy must be included in P; any other resident rules would have to be counted too.
If an intermediate configuration has more rules than B, does that alone violate the bound?

Not necessarily. The limit is 2B, not B. An intermediate configuration could exceed B but still fit beneath 2B on its own. The question then becomes what other rules coexist with it at the switch, including rules in the other bank.
What if the intermediate configuration by itself needs more than 2B rules at one switch?

If all of those rules have to be present at that switch simultaneously, that configuration alone would exceed the stated peak limit. Two banks cannot repair that arithmetic. Whether the routing work can avoid such simultaneous occupancy is not specified by the question.
Can you give a simple arithmetic illustration without assuming anything about our actual switches?

As a purely illustrative case, suppose a switch has 10 rules initially and 10 finally, giving a peak allowance of 20. If one intermediate bank needs 15 rules while another resident bank needs 10, those banks total 25, above the allowance. If the other bank instead needs 4, the total is 19, so the intermediate bank’s being larger than an endpoint would not alone exceed the limit. Neither illustration describes a measured system.
Would serializing the overlapping updates prevent the 15-plus-10 situation?

Not merely by serializing them. Even with only one overlapping update being advanced at a time, an earlier bank might still need to remain available while the next configuration is prepared. Serialization concerns update ordering; rule occupancy also depends on which configurations must coexist and when their rules can be removed.
So does “dual” mean the peak can never be more than twice an endpoint?

No. Two banks limit the number of banks being discussed, not the number of rules in each bank. If an intermediate bank is larger than the relevant endpoint counts, the sum of two bank sizes can exceed twice the larger endpoint count. The factor of two in the requirement is a rule-count bound, not a consequence that follows just from having two banks.
Could sharing identical rules between the banks change the arithmetic?

It could affect actual occupancy if the switch stores a shared rule only once, but the question does not specify such sharing. The safe comparison is against rules actually resident at the switch. Counting a rule twice when it is stored once, or once when it occupies two entries, would both misstate the peak.
Does waiting for draining before moving on settle the bound?

Waiting can affect how many old rules coexist with new ones, but it does not establish the bound by itself. A single oversized intermediate configuration might still exceed the allowance, and a permitted pair of banks might have a combined count above it. Draining and the capacity comparison address related but different conditions.
Should the check be per intermediate transition or only over the entire sequence of serialized updates?

The peak requirement concerns the maximum at each switch during the relevant update sequence, including intermediate transitions. Checking only the initial and final installed states would miss a transient excess. For any proposed sequence, the occupancy at every stage where rules coexist must remain at or below the stated per-switch allowance.
What if someone treats each queued update’s local endpoints as its own allowance?

That does not, by itself, answer the question about a bound expressed using the initial and final configurations of the update sequence under consideration. Changing which endpoints define the comparison could change the numerical allowance. The scope of “initial” and “final” must therefore be kept explicit, rather than silently replacing the stated bound with a separate allowance for every queued step.
Are we saying the proposed banks cannot meet the bound?

No categorical conclusion follows from the question alone. They can stay within the bound if their actual peak per-switch occupancy does not exceed 2× max(initial, final). Larger intermediate configurations make that condition nontrivial, and some possible occupancies would violate it. No counts for a particular update sequence are supplied here.
What would need to be compared before claiming the bound is satisfied?

For each switch, identify the stated initial and final rule counts, determine their maximum, and compare twice that value with the greatest number of rules simultaneously resident during the serialized updates—including intermediate banks and rules still retained while draining. Without those peak counts, dual banking and serialization alone do not establish compliance.
Is the packet-consistency question the same as this capacity question?

No. A dual-bank transition might keep each packet on one committed configuration while still exceeding the per-switch rule limit. Conversely, a rule-count calculation alone says nothing about which configuration a packet follows. The question here is whether the bank occupancy remains within 2× max(initial, final) despite larger intermediate configurations.

For the dual-bank capacity question, I propose coalescing oversized intermediate intents before commit. Then admit a transition only if the combined bank rules stay within 2× max(initial, final) at each switch.

That plan addresses the possibility that serialized, overlapping updates produce an intermediate configuration larger than the endpoints. Coalescing happens before an oversized intermediate intent is committed; admission then checks the combined rules in the banks against the per-switch bound. It is a proposed capacity discipline, not yet a measurement or proof that every requested transition can be admitted.
What is an “intermediate intent” in this plan?

It is a proposed routing state between the initial and final configurations of the update sequence. The concern is an intermediate state whose rule footprint makes the dual-bank transition too large. Calling it an intent matters: the plan calls for coalescing it before commit, rather than first committing an oversized state and trying to repair its rule count afterward.
Does coalescing mean we discard an update request?

That is not stated. The plan says to coalesce oversized intermediate intents, but it does not define the coalescing operation or authorize dropping requested routing changes. Its stated purpose here is to avoid committing an intermediate configuration whose bank occupancy would exceed the bound.
Could we commit the intermediate configuration and coalesce it later if admission fails?

That would reverse the specified order. The plan puts coalescing before commit and admits transitions only if their combined bank rules stay within the limit. A later reduction would not undo a peak-rule violation that occurred during the transition.
How should admission calculate the limit?

For each switch, take its initial rule count I and final rule count F and set the allowance to 2 × max(I, F). Compare that allowance with the rules the two banks would have simultaneously for the proposed transition. The admission condition must hold at each switch; spare capacity at one switch does not offset excess rules at another.
Why count the banks together instead of checking each bank separately?

The requirement limits peak rules present at a switch, not the size of either bank in isolation. Two banks could each look acceptable individually while their combined rules exceed 2× max(initial, final). Admission therefore needs to consider their simultaneous occupancy.
If an intermediate bank exceeds max(initial, final), is it automatically rejected?

No. The condition is on the combined bank rules compared with twice the larger endpoint count. An intermediate bank may be larger than either endpoint yet still leave enough room for the other bank. Conversely, a smaller intermediate bank could be part of a pair whose combined occupancy exceeds the allowance.
Could you illustrate the admission check without asserting actual switch counts?

As an arithmetic illustration only, if a switch has 10 rules initially and 12 finally, its allowance is 2 × 12 = 24. Proposed banks containing 13 and 10 rules would total 23 and pass this particular check; banks containing 13 and 12 would total 25 and fail it. Those numbers are not measurements of the proposed system.
What happens to an intent that fails the combined-bank check?

The plan does not admit that transition as proposed. It calls for coalescing oversized intermediate intents before commit, then applying the capacity condition. It does not specify exactly how to revise a failing intent, how many attempts to make, or what happens if no admissible transition can be formed.
Does coalescing guarantee that every oversized intermediate intent becomes small enough?

No such guarantee is stated. Coalescing is the planned response to oversized intermediate intents; whether it yields a transition whose combined bank rules meet the bound remains to be checked by admission. The plan should not be described as having solved every possible capacity case in advance.
Could the admission check be made once for the whole network?

It must preserve the per-switch comparison. A network-wide total or average cannot establish that each switch stays within 2× max(initial, final). The proposed transition needs the combined-bank check wherever its rules may be resident.
What about rules still present while an earlier configuration drains?

They matter to actual peak occupancy. The plan’s combined-bank admission condition cannot be applied as though a bank were empty when its rules are still resident. Whether an earlier bank remains occupied affects which transition can pass the check; the plan does not specify a separate accounting procedure for that situation.
Does serialization make the check unnecessary once intents are coalesced?

No. Serialization orders overlapping updates, while coalescing addresses oversized intermediate intents. Neither alone establishes the combined size of the banks during a transition. Admission remains the explicit capacity gate in this plan.
If the combined bank count is exactly 2× max(initial, final), can the transition pass?

Yes, with respect to the stated numerical condition: “within 2×” includes equality. It would still need to satisfy the system’s other requirements, and the calculation must reflect the rules actually present at each switch.
Does passing admission mean the transition must immediately commit?

No. “Admit transitions only if” makes the rule-count check a necessary condition for admission, not a promise of immediate commitment whenever it passes. The plan does not give a commit schedule or specify all other conditions for proceeding.
Does this plan establish per-packet consistency too?

Not by itself. Coalescing before commit and checking combined bank rules address the capacity concern raised by larger intermediate configurations. They do not, on their own, establish how packets select a committed configuration or remain on it throughout a path.
And can we claim updates will complete after controller connectivity recovers?

Not from this plan alone. The capacity gate may determine that a proposed transition cannot proceed as formed, and no general method for resolving every such case is specified. The plan states how to avoid admitting an over-budget dual-bank transition; it does not provide a completion result.
What is the precise plan, without claiming it has already worked?

Coalesce oversized intermediate intents before commit, and admit a transition only when the combined bank rules at each switch stay within 2× max(initial, final). Whether this produces admissible transitions for all requested updates remains to be established.

I propose coalescing overlapping routing intents into committed snapshots, reserving per-switch shadow capacity before activating each snapshot through epoch-tagged ingress rules. How should I understand the proposal as a whole?

It separates forming a configuration from letting packets use it. Overlapping intents are coalesced into a snapshot that is committed. Before activation, the system reserves shadow capacity at each switch for the rules the transition needs. Epoch-tagged ingress rules then select the snapshot for packets entering the network. The proposal names that sequence, but does not yet specify how intents are combined, how capacity is calculated, or a complete activation protocol.
What is being coalesced: packets, routes, or update requests?

The proposal says to coalesce overlapping intents—the requested routing changes—into committed snapshots. It does not say to combine packets or their paths. A snapshot represents a routing configuration that packets can be associated with once it is committed and activated for ingress use.
Does coalescing mean each overlapping request gets its own committed snapshot?

Not necessarily. Coalescing suggests forming a snapshot from overlapping intents rather than assuming a separate snapshot for each request. The proposal does not specify which requests are grouped together, how conflicts between their intents are resolved, or how many snapshots result.
Could I say every requested intent is preserved exactly as submitted?

That is not established here. The proposal calls for coalescing overlapping intents, but does not define the resulting snapshot’s relationship to every individual request. It would be premature to claim either exact preservation or the removal of any requested change.
Why call the resulting configurations “committed snapshots”?

“Snapshot” conveys a configuration that can be treated as a coherent whole, rather than a packet encountering parts of different in-progress changes. “Committed” matters because the packet-level goal is for each packet to follow one committed routing configuration. The proposal does not define the storage operation or decision procedure that makes a snapshot committed.
Is committing a snapshot the same thing as activating it?

No. The wording distinguishes them: intents are coalesced into committed snapshots, shadow capacity is reserved before activation, and activation occurs through epoch-tagged ingress rules. A snapshot’s being committed does not, by itself, say that ingress has begun selecting it for new packets.
What does “shadow capacity” mean in this proposal?

It is capacity reserved at a switch for the rule footprint needed while a snapshot is being brought into use alongside routing state that may still be present. The proposal makes that reservation a prerequisite to activation. It does not specify the reservation representation, exact accounting method, or number of shadow rules at any switch.
Does reserving capacity mean the shadow rules have already been installed?

Not necessarily. A reservation is a capacity commitment; installed rules are actual switch entries. The proposal says to reserve per-switch shadow capacity before activation, but does not equate reserving it with installing every rule or specify when installation occurs.
Why make the reservation per switch instead of looking at available capacity across the network?

The rule constraint is per switch: peak rules at each switch must stay within 2× max(initial, final). Spare capacity elsewhere cannot compensate for one switch exceeding its own limit. Reserving capacity per switch is therefore aligned with the location where the constraint applies.
Does this proposal already prove that 2× max(initial, final) will be respected?

No. Reservation before activation is a proposed way to avoid activating a snapshot without room for its shadow rules. To establish the bound, the reservation and actual occupancy would need to account for all rules simultaneously present at each switch and compare the peak with 2× max(initial, final) for that switch. The proposal supplies no counts or proof.
If an intermediate snapshot is larger than both the initial and final configurations, could the reservation still pass?

That depends on the combined per-switch footprint during its transition, not just the intermediate snapshot’s size alone. The requirement limits the peak to twice the larger endpoint rule count. The proposal does not state that coalescing always makes an intermediate snapshot small enough; the capacity reservation must be assessed against the actual rules that would coexist.
Does a capacity reservation for one snapshot automatically cover another snapshot waiting behind it?

No such sharing is specified. The proposal says to reserve per-switch shadow capacity before activating each snapshot. If rules associated with different snapshots could coexist, their effect on actual switch occupancy would need to be considered; a reservation for one snapshot cannot simply be assumed to cover every other one.
What activates a snapshot for packets?

The proposal specifies activation through epoch-tagged ingress rules. Conceptually, ingress selects an epoch for a packet so the packet can be associated with the corresponding committed snapshot. It does not specify a tag format, whether ingresses change simultaneously, or the exact commands used to activate those rules.
If different packets enter with different epoch tags, is that inconsistent?

Not by itself. Per-packet consistency allows different packets to follow different committed configurations. The important condition is that each packet’s forwarding decisions correspond to one committed snapshot throughout its path; seeing more than one epoch among packets is not itself a mixed-version path.
Do epoch-tagged ingress rules alone ensure a packet stays with its snapshot at every switch?

Not alone. An ingress tag identifies the intended snapshot, but the rules that handle that tag along the packet’s path must also correspond to that committed snapshot and remain available while needed. The proposal identifies ingress-based activation; it does not spell out the full downstream rule or packet-draining protocol.
Would it be safe to activate a snapshot first and find out afterward whether there is shadow capacity?

That would reverse the proposal’s explicit ordering. Per-switch shadow capacity is to be reserved before activating each snapshot. Checking afterward could allow packets to select a snapshot before the capacity needed to support its rules has been accounted for.
Does a successful reservation require immediate activation?
No. The proposal makes reservation a prerequisite, not a command to activate immediately. It does not specify when a reserved snapshot is activated or what other checks, if any, precede activation.
How does the proposal relate to overlapping updates being concurrent?

It accommodates the presence of overlapping intents by coalescing them into committed snapshots, rather than assuming every request affects disjoint routing state. It does not specify how much preparation runs concurrently, the order of resulting snapshots, or how long an overlapping request waits.
Can we say coalescing guarantees that all overlapping requests eventually complete?

No. Coalescing describes how overlapping intents would be represented for commitment; it does not establish that every requested change can be formed into an admissible snapshot or that every update completes. Completion after controller connectivity recovers remains a system requirement, not a result established by this proposal alone.
Does this proposal specify what happens if the controller crashes between commitment and ingress activation?

Not in detail. It distinguishes a committed snapshot from activating it through ingress rules, which makes that interval meaningful, but it does not state how a restarted controller determines which ingresses activated the snapshot or how it resumes. Those crash-recovery details would be needed to establish the broader packet-consistency and completion guarantees.
Should I assume the capacity reservation itself survives a controller crash?

The proposal does not say. Before claiming crash-safe activation or recovery, a design would need to explain what happens to reservation information across a crash and how it relates to actual switch occupancy. No particular persistence mechanism is specified here.
How does this differ from simply checking that a committed snapshot fits by itself?

The proposed reservation is for per-switch shadow capacity before activation, so the relevant question is what must coexist during the transition. A snapshot might fit a switch in isolation while its rules plus other resident rules exceed the peak allowance. Checking the snapshot alone would not necessarily account for that combined occupancy.
If a snapshot cannot obtain enough shadow capacity at one switch, what outcome does the proposal prescribe?

It does not prescribe a complete fallback. It does prescribe an ordering: reserve per-switch shadow capacity before activating each snapshot. If that capacity cannot be reserved, the proposal does not authorize treating the prerequisite as satisfied; it does not say whether to revise the snapshot, wait, or take some other action.
Can you restate the proposal without implying its guarantees have already been demonstrated?

Coalesce overlapping routing intents into committed snapshots. Before activating each snapshot, reserve the necessary shadow capacity at each switch; then use epoch-tagged ingress rules to select that snapshot for packets. This is a proposed structure for update and capacity control, not yet a proof of the 2× max(initial, final) rule bound, per-packet consistency through crashes, or completion after connectivity recovers.

I want to put the routing design into an operational plan: merge overlapping intents; admit dual rule banks within 2× endpoint budgets; journal commits; flip reserved epoch tags; drain; and reconcile after controller crashes. How do these steps fit together?

They form a proposed update and recovery sequence. Merging intents produces a configuration to consider. Before activating it, admission checks whether the dual banks fit the per-switch rule budget. A commit is journaled before reserved epoch tags are flipped at ingress. Draining addresses rules still needed by packets associated with an older configuration, while reconciliation addresses the state left by a controller crash. The sequence is intended to serve per-packet consistency, bounded switch occupancy, and eventual completion after connectivity recovers; stating it does not yet prove those outcomes.
What exactly are we merging?

The inputs are routing intents, including ones that overlap. The plan is to merge them into a configuration that can be considered for admission and commitment, rather than assume intersecting requests can each proceed independently. It does not define the merge rule, the number of intents in a merge, or how conflicting requests are resolved.
Does merging the intents mean the resulting configuration is already committed?

No. Merging forms the proposed configuration; journaling the commit is a later step. Admission also comes between them in the stated plan. A merged intent should not be treated as a configuration that packets may follow solely because the merge has been formed.
What does the admission step need to check?

It checks the combined rule occupancy of the dual banks against the endpoint budget at each switch. For a switch with initial rule count I and final rule count F, the stated peak limit is 2 × max(I, F). Admission cannot examine the proposed new bank in isolation if rules in the other bank will also be present.
Why use the larger endpoint count rather than adding the endpoint counts?

Because the specified bound is 2× max(initial, final), applied per switch. Adding the initial and final counts would be a different numerical test. The admission check must also consider the actual combined bank rules that would be resident, including a larger intermediate configuration if one is proposed.
If one switch passes and another fails, can the transition still be admitted?

Not under a per-switch admission condition. The combined banks must fit within that switch’s 2× endpoint budget at every switch where the transition requires rules. Unused room at one switch does not offset an over-budget switch.
Does the word “admit” mean every merged set of intents will eventually fit?

No. The plan says to admit dual-bank transitions within the budget; it does not establish that every possible merge will satisfy that condition or specify what to do when one does not. The capacity gate must not be confused with a guarantee that all proposed configurations are admissible.
Why journal the commit before flipping a tag?

The ordering distinguishes a committed routing configuration from one that ingress could select before commitment was recorded. Once an ingress tag flips, packets may enter associated with the selected epoch. Journaling the commit first is meant to keep that activation tied to a committed configuration and provide information for recovery after a controller crash.
Does a journaled commit prove that the ingress flip happened?

No. The commit records one step; the ingress flip changes what an ingress selects. A crash could interrupt work between those steps or while flips are underway. That is why reconciliation after a crash has a separate role: it must account for actual ingress state rather than infer every flip from the commit record.
What makes a tag “reserved” in this plan?

A reserved epoch tag is not available for reuse as the identifier of another configuration while its reservation remains in force. That matters when packets associated with an earlier use of a tag may still require old rules. The plan calls for flipping reserved tags, but does not set out the reservation record, release procedure, or exact tag format.
Could a tag be flipped merely because it is reserved, before admission and commitment?

That would not follow the proposed order. Reservation identifies an available tag for the transition; it does not substitute for the dual-bank admission check or the journaled commit. In the stated plan, merging and admission precede commit journaling, which precedes flipping the reserved tags.
Does “flip reserved tags” require every ingress to change simultaneously?

No simultaneous flip is specified. The plan identifies epoch-tagged ingress activation but does not define atomicity across ingresses. Its packet-level objective is that each packet follow one committed routing configuration even if different packets enter under different epochs.
Where does draining enter once ingress starts selecting the committed configuration?

Draining addresses packets that may still be using the earlier configuration. Changing what ingress selects for later packets does not establish that earlier packets no longer need their rules. The plan therefore includes a drain stage rather than treating an ingress flip as permission to remove old rules immediately.
Does the plan specify how we know draining is finished?

It does not spell out a drain procedure here. Drain acknowledgments are part of the design context, but this plan only names draining as a stage. It does not specify who acknowledges it, the evidence behind an acknowledgment, or the precise rule-removal operation.
If a controller crash occurs while tags are being flipped, do we skip ahead to draining on restart?

The plan calls for reconciliation after crashes, so recovery cannot simply assume the intended flips all took effect and proceed on that assumption. It needs to account for the state left by the crash before taking actions that depend on which epochs packets may have used. The plan does not provide a detailed reconciliation algorithm or a universal ordering for every possible crash point.
What information is reconciliation trying to align?

Conceptually, it aligns the recorded commit and intended update with the ingress epoch state that actually exists after the crash, while accounting for rules that packets may still need. A journaled commit and an intended flip do not alone identify what each ingress selected. The plan names reconciliation as the recovery step without prescribing the exact queries or records it uses.
Does reconciliation replace the capacity check when the controller reconnects?

No. They answer different questions. Admission constrains how many bank rules may coexist at each switch; reconciliation deals with the update state after a crash. Recovery actions must still respect the rule budget, but the plan does not provide detailed accounting for every recovery state.
Which step is responsible for ensuring every packet follows one committed configuration?

No single named step is sufficient alone. A journaled commit distinguishes a committed configuration, and epoch-tagged ingress activation is intended to associate packets with it. Maintaining the corresponding rules while packets need them, including through draining and crash recovery, is also necessary. The plan assembles these responsibilities, but their combination still needs a complete correctness argument.
Does this plan say updates finish even if controller connectivity never returns?

No. The system requirement is completion after controller connectivity recovers. Reconciliation is the planned way to resume coherently after crashes, but this statement neither requires completion during a continuing disconnection nor reports that completion has been established for every update.
Can I describe the whole thing as a verified protocol now?

Not from this plan alone. It specifies an intended sequence and capacity gate: merge overlapping intents, admit dual banks only within each switch’s 2× max(initial, final) endpoint budget, journal commits, flip reserved epoch tags, drain, and reconcile after crashes. It does not report verification of the peak rule bound, packet consistency, or completion for all executions.
Implement an intent coalescer atop EpochReconciler v0.1 that reserves shadow-bank capacity under each switch’s 2× endpoint-rule cap.

The implementation activity is to add an intent coalescer on top of EpochReconciler v0.1. It should bring overlapping routing intents together and reserve capacity for shadow-bank rules, subject to a separate 2× endpoint-rule cap at every switch. This states what to implement; it does not say the coalescer has been completed or tested.
What is the coalescer responsible for in that description?

Its stated responsibilities are coalescing intents and reserving shadow-bank capacity within the cap. Coalescing concerns the proposed routing configuration; reservation concerns whether the switch has room for the rules that would be present during a transition. The activity does not specify an algorithm for combining intents or a data structure for reservations.
Why build it atop EpochReconciler v0.1?

That identifies the component it builds on. EpochReconciler v0.1 supplies commit journaling, ingress-tag polling, idempotent flip replay, and old-rule removal after drain acknowledgments. The coalescer’s additional responsibility here is intent handling and shadow-bank capacity reservation; the activity does not describe a new implementation of those reconciliation functions.
Does the coalescer decide which epoch an ingress is currently using?

That is not one of its specified new responsibilities. Ingress-tag polling is a capability of EpochReconciler v0.1. Saying the coalescer is built atop it does not establish a particular interface between them or mean that a capacity reservation determines an ingress’s current tag.

Durability means recovery can rely on its recorded identity and relevant committed state rather than solely on controller memory lost in a crash. The proposal does not name a storage system, record format, or exact durability protocol.

It means recovery is intended to be able to resume or repeat appropriate epoch-related work after interruption without treating a controller crash as the end of the update. No. Replay concerns continuing work associated with an epoch after interruption; it need not mean inventing a different configuration. Its packet-level purpose would be to preserve the association with a committed configuration while recovery proceeds. The exact replay semantics remain unspecified.
How do durability and replayability help with controller crashes?

Durability is intended to preserve the information recovery needs, and replayability is intended to let recovery continue work that a crash interrupted. Neither property alone proves that every packet follows one committed configuration or that every update completes after connectivity returns. The recovery procedure would still need to respect the actual ingress and rule state.

Not as stated. It is the condition for reusing a tag. A tag should not be assigned a new configuration meaning until network-wide packet quiescence has been established for packets that could still depend on its earlier meaning. The proposal does not say that forming or committing every epoch requires the whole network to be quiescent.
