The proposal expressly conditions tag reuse on network-wide packet quiescence. Its safety concern is whether a packet associated with the tag’s earlier meaning could still reach rules after the tag is recycled. It does not define the relationship between a drain acknowledgment and quiescence or say how quiescence is detected.
Does network-wide quiescence necessarily mean that no packets of any kind can be present anywhere?

The proposal does not define it that narrowly or specify a detection method. For safe tag reuse, the relevant property is that no packet anywhere in the network can still depend on that tag’s earlier configuration meaning. We should not silently replace that property with an unstated measurement or assume it has already been achieved.
Could an ingress stop issuing a tag and immediately release it?

Stopping assignment to new packets does not by itself establish network-wide packet quiescence. Packets already carrying the tag could still be relevant. Under this proposal, reuse waits for the network-wide condition rather than following immediately from an ingress change.
Would it be a violation if two packets carry different epoch tags at the same time?

No. Per-packet consistency does not require all packets to use the same committed configuration simultaneously. The concern is that an individual packet must not start under one committed configuration and later be handled as if its tag identified another. The quiescence condition is directed at that risk when tags are reused.
Does a durable epoch make its numerical tag permanent?

No permanent tag assignment is stated. Epoch durability concerns recoverable configuration identity and state; tag reuse is permitted by the proposal, but only after network-wide packet quiescence. The proposal does not specify an epoch-number space or a schedule for recycling tags.
What is classifier-inclusive admission admitting?

It is the rule-capacity check before proceeding with rule changes: projected peak occupancy at each switch must fit the 2× endpoint-rule limit, with ingress classifiers counted rather than excluded because they are not routing-bank entries. The proposal does not give a particular admission algorithm or rule-inventory format.
Can you state that limit precisely?

At each switch, let I be its initial rule count, F its final rule count, and P its peak rule count. The required comparison is P ≤ 2 × max(I, F). Classifier-inclusive admission must account for classifier entries that contribute to P. This is a per-switch bound, not an average over the network.
If there are two banks, could admission check only the shadow bank and then separately check classifiers?

Separate bookkeeping could be used, but the decisive comparison must cover their combined simultaneous occupancy at the switch. A bank count and a classifier count can each look acceptable alone while their total exceeds the cap. The proposal does not prescribe the bookkeeping method.
What about rules that appear briefly during replacement?

They contribute to peak occupancy if they coexist with other entries at a switch. A classifier-inclusive check should not be mistaken for permission to disregard other resident rules. The proposal explicitly names classifiers, but does not spell out a particular reservation or replacement procedure; compliance ultimately concerns the total peak per switch.
Does exactly 2× max(initial, final) pass admission?

Yes, as far as that numerical bound is concerned: the limit permits equality and prohibits a peak above it. Admission must use the relevant switch’s own endpoint counts and include rules that will actually be resident together.
Can spare rule capacity at another switch offset one switch going above its limit?
No. The constraint is per switch. If one switch’s projected peak exceeds 2× max(initial, final) for that switch, lower occupancy elsewhere does not satisfy its bound.

Not from admission alone. I propose fencing rebooted switches until their old rule banks have been replayed, requiring queue-aware drain certificates before epoch tags are reused, and retaining classifier-inclusive admission under the per-switch 2× rule cap. How do those pieces fit together?

They put separate conditions on recovery, tag reuse, and rule capacity. The fence prevents a rebooted switch from being treated as ready for the relevant epoch traffic before its old banks have been replayed. A queue-aware drain certificate is the proposed prerequisite for reusing a tag, so queued packets that might still carry its earlier meaning are accounted for. Classifier-inclusive admission remains the check against peak rules exceeding 2× max(initial, final) at each switch. This is a proposal, not a demonstrated guarantee.
Why specifically replay the old banks at a rebooted switch?

Packets already associated with an older committed configuration may still need the rules for that configuration. Replaying the old banks is intended to restore those rules before the switch is allowed to handle traffic that depends on them. The proposal does not specify where the replay data comes from or how the switch confirms that replay is complete.
Does fencing mean the switch must drop all packets during replay?

No such behavior is specified. The proposal requires fencing the rebooted switch until its old banks are replayed, but does not define whether fencing blocks, holds, redirects, or otherwise constrains traffic. Its safety purpose is to avoid exposing relevant packets to an incompletely restored rule bank; a particular packet-handling policy cannot be inferred from the word “fence” alone.
Could we lift the fence as soon as the controller starts replaying the banks?

That would not meet the stated condition. The fence lasts until the old banks have been replayed, not merely until replay begins or is requested. The proposal does not define the evidence needed to decide that replay has finished.
If the newer configuration is available, can the rebooted switch ignore its old banks?

The proposal does not make that exception. A packet admitted under an older committed configuration may still depend on its old bank even when rules for a newer configuration exist. The stated fence remains in place until the old banks have been replayed.
Is replay of the old banks the same as proving old packets have drained?

No. Replay concerns making the old forwarding rules available after reboot. Draining concerns whether any packet still needs the old configuration or an epoch tag's earlier meaning. The proposal treats them as distinct: replay is the condition for lifting the reboot fence, while a queue-aware drain certificate is required before tag reuse.
What makes a drain certificate queue-aware?

It must account for packets that could remain buffered or queued, rather than conclude that draining is complete solely from an observation that overlooks them. The proposal does not define which queues are checked, how their contents are identified, or how the certificate is issued. “Queue-aware” names the property the certificate needs, not an already specified measurement procedure.
Would a zero in-flight counter alone qualify as that certificate?

Not automatically. If a packet can remain queued without being represented by that counter, the zero would not establish the queue-aware drain condition. A counter could contribute to a certificate only insofar as its stated semantics actually cover the relevant packets; those semantics are not supplied in this proposal.
Does a queue-aware certificate need to identify the epoch tag?

For the proposed tag-reuse decision, its claim must be applicable to the tag being considered. Evidence about packets associated with another tag would not establish that this tag's earlier use has drained. The proposal does not specify a certificate format or how a queue's packets are associated with tags.
Does the certificate allow the old bank to be removed immediately?

The explicit condition here is that a queue-aware drain certificate is required before tag reuse. The proposal does not separately state a rule-removal procedure or timing. Tag reuse, bank replay, and removing old entries should not be treated as identical operations.
What if the old banks are fully replayed but the drain certificate has not been obtained?

Completing bank replay would satisfy the stated condition for the reboot fence, but not the stated prerequisite for tag reuse. The tag must still wait for a queue-aware drain certificate. The proposal does not prescribe what other update work may proceed during that wait.
And if a drain certificate exists while a rebooted switch's old banks have not yet been replayed?

The certificate cannot substitute for the replay condition on the rebooted switch. The proposal calls for fencing that switch until its old banks are replayed, separately from requiring the certificate before recycling a tag. How a certificate's validity is established across a reboot is not specified.
Could a packet still be buffered after a certificate says the tag has drained?

A sound queue-aware certificate for that tag would have to exclude any queued packet that could still depend on its earlier meaning. Whether an implementation can establish that, including through a reboot, is an open correctness question. The proposal should not be stated as evidence that no such packet exists.
Why not just wait a fixed amount of time before recycling the tag?

This proposal makes a queue-aware drain certificate, rather than passage of a fixed time, the condition for reuse. A time interval by itself would not explain whether relevant queued packets have drained. No numerical packet-lifetime threshold is specified here.
What exactly is risky about reusing a tag too soon?

A packet still carrying the tag from its earlier use might encounter rules that interpret it as belonging to a later committed configuration. If that packet previously followed decisions from its original configuration, its path could mix versions. The certificate is proposed to prevent that possibility by establishing the appropriate drain condition before the tag receives a new meaning.
Does having multiple committed configurations active at different ingresses violate per-packet consistency?

Not by itself. Different packets can follow different committed configurations. The requirement is that an individual packet follow one committed configuration along its path. Replaying old banks and postponing tag reuse are intended to preserve that distinction through a switch reboot and subsequent updates.
What does classifier-inclusive admission retain from the capacity side of the design?

It keeps ingress-classifier rule entries in the capacity calculation. The requirement is that each switch's peak number of rules be no greater than 2× max(initial, final), using that switch's endpoint rule counts. Checking only routing-bank entries would not account for classifiers resident at the same time.
Are replayed old-bank rules exempt from that 2× cap because they are needed for recovery?

No exemption is stated. Replayed old-bank rules, shadow-bank rules, ingress classifiers, and other entries that are simultaneously resident all matter to actual peak occupancy. The proposal retains classifier-inclusive 2× admission while adding the replay and certificate conditions; recovery does not relax the per-switch limit.
Do buffered packets themselves count as switch rules for that limit?

No. Buffered packets are relevant to whether a tag can safely be reused, while the 2× bound counts rule entries present at a switch. Keeping banks available for those packets can affect how many rules coexist, but the packets are not themselves rule entries in that comparison.
Could admission approve a replay just by counting the old bank in isolation?

That would not establish the peak bound if classifiers or other banks are present alongside it. The per-switch comparison must reflect the total rules simultaneously resident during the proposed actions. The proposal does not give a detailed admission algorithm for replay or say what to do if sufficient capacity is unavailable.
Does the proposal establish that updates always complete once controller connectivity recovers?

Not yet. It sets conditions for safe recovery and tag reuse, but does not specify how bank replay, certificates, and capacity admission can always be completed after connectivity returns. Completion remains a requirement to establish, not a result implied merely by naming these safeguards.

It is more accurate to describe it as a proposal aimed at those guarantees. Fencing rebooted switches until old banks replay and requiring queue-aware drain certificates before tag reuse target per-packet consistency; classifier-inclusive admission targets the per-switch 2× max(initial, final) peak-rule limit. Their combined correctness and recovery progress are not established by the proposal alone.

Fence each rebooted switch until its old rule banks are replayed; reuse epoch tags only after queue-aware drain certificates; and retain classifier-inclusive admission under the per-switch peak limit of 2× max(initial, final).

For the dual-bank capacity problem, the plan is to coalesce oversized intents into endpoint snapshots and reserve capacity for both banks, classifiers, and replacements before each 2×-capped transition. How should that work conceptually?

The plan has two parts. First, coalesce intents that would otherwise produce an oversized intermediate configuration into endpoint snapshots for proposed transitions. Second, before each transition, reserve enough per-switch capacity for the rules that may coexist: both banks, ingress classifiers, and transient replacement entries. A transition proceeds under this plan only if its projected peak fits within 2× max(initial, final) at every affected switch. This is a plan, not evidence that every set of intents can be coalesced into an admissible transition.
What makes an intent “oversized” here?

In this context, it is an intent whose proposed intermediate rule footprint would make a transition exceed the relevant per-switch capacity budget when all coexisting rules are counted. Size cannot be judged from the intermediate routing bank alone: the other bank, classifiers, and replacements also matter. No numerical rule counts for a particular intent are specified.
What does “coalesce into endpoint snapshots” mean without defining a merge algorithm?

It means forming proposed transition endpoints from the intents rather than requiring each oversized intermediate intent to become a separately installed configuration. The plan does not say which intents are combined, exactly how their routing choices are reconciled, or how many endpoint snapshots result. Coalescing is a proposed way to avoid an over-budget intermediate step, subject to the same capacity check.
Does that mean we can skip committing any intermediate state whatsoever?

The plan does not specify a universal rule about all intermediate states. It says to coalesce oversized intents into endpoint snapshots. We should not extend that to a claim that no intermediate configuration will ever be needed, or that every requested routing change can be represented without one.
Could coalescing simply discard one of the oversized intents?

Discarding an intent is not stated. The plan names coalescing as the response to oversized intents but leaves its precise semantics open. It should not be read as permission to silently omit a requested change, nor as a guarantee that every combination of intents can be represented successfully.
Why do the capacity reservations have to happen before each transition?

They are intended to prevent a transition from installing rules that push a switch over its limit. Checking only after installation could discover a peak violation after it has already occurred. The plan therefore places the combined capacity check before each 2×-capped transition rather than treating a reservation made for a different transition as sufficient.
Is it enough to reserve capacity for the destination bank?

No. The plan explicitly includes both banks. During a transition, rules for another configuration may remain resident while rules for the destination are present. The per-switch peak is determined by what coexists, not by the new bank's size in isolation.
Does having only two banks automatically make their total fit within twice the larger endpoint?

No. The number of banks does not limit the size of each bank. In particular, an oversized intermediate bank could make the combined occupancy exceed 2× max(initial, final). That is why the plan pairs coalescing with an explicit reservation for all relevant rule entries.
Why list classifiers separately from the two banks?

Classifiers can occupy rule entries at a switch without being counted as entries in either routing bank. Because the limit concerns peak switch rules, their slots must be included if they coexist with the banks. Listing them separately helps prevent an apparently acceptable two-bank estimate from understating total occupancy.
And what do “replacements” contribute?

Replacing an entry may temporarily leave both its old and new versions resident. The reservation needs to cover any additional entries that can coexist during that process. The plan does not specify the replacement order, how many replacements overlap, or an allocation method; the relevant quantity is their contribution to the greatest simultaneous rule count.
Should we just sum every rule that appears at any time across the transition?

No. That would count entries that might never coexist. The capacity comparison is against the projected peak number simultaneously resident at each switch. It must include all entries that can be present together, while avoiding double-counting the same stored entry or adding states that occur at different times.
Suppose a classifier is already present in the initial endpoint count. Do we add it a second time?

The initial count helps set the numerical cap; the projected occupancy is a separate count of actual entries present during the transition. A classifier already resident contributes one occupied slot at a given instant, not two merely because it also appears in an endpoint count. An additional classifier or replacement entry that can coexist would require its own slot.
Can you write the bound for one switch?

Let I and F be that switch's initial and final rule counts for the transition under consideration, and let P be its greatest simultaneous rule occupancy during that transition. The admission target is P ≤ 2 × max(I, F). P must account for the resident entries in both banks, classifiers, and any additional replacement entries that coexist at the peak.
If a bank is larger than max(I, F), must we reject the transition immediately?

Not solely on that fact. The cap is twice max(I, F), and the check is on combined occupancy. A bank larger than max(I, F) could still fit if the other resident entries leave enough room; alternatively, smaller individual banks could exceed the cap together. The plan requires the full per-switch comparison.
What if the combined banks already consume the entire 2× allowance?

If classifiers or additional replacement entries would be resident at the same time, there would be no room for them under that allowance. The transition could not be admitted in that projected form. If a particular entry is shared or absent at the peak, the actual occupancy calculation must reflect that; the plan does not prescribe a specific way of changing an over-budget transition.
Is an occupancy projection exactly equal to the 2× cap acceptable?
Yes. A 2×-capped transition allows equality; it does not allow a projected peak greater than 2 × max(initial, final) for any affected switch.
Could a switch with plenty of spare slots offset another switch that fails?

No. This is a per-switch condition. Each switch must have sufficient reserved capacity for its own combined occupancy; spare capacity elsewhere cannot compensate for a local peak above its 2× endpoint cap.
Would a single capacity reservation cover a whole queue of future transitions?

The stated plan calls for reserving capacity before each transition. It does not say that one reservation automatically covers later transitions, whose endpoint snapshots and coexisting rules may differ. Each proposed transition needs to meet the applicable per-switch check.
What if an old bank is still present when we consider the next endpoint snapshot?

If it remains resident during the proposed next transition, its entries count toward that transition's projected occupancy. Admission cannot assume those slots are free until the entries are actually absent when the new rules would coexist. The plan does not define when an old bank is removed.
Could admission consider only the starting and ending table sizes?

No. Classifiers, both banks, and temporary replacements could create a larger peak between those states. The plan specifically reserves for their coexistence before allowing each transition, so an endpoint-only measurement would not fully address the peak constraint.
Can you give a small illustrative calculation without implying we measured any switch?

Purely hypothetically, if a switch had 10 rules initially and 12 finally, the cap for that transition would be 24. If two banks would hold 9 and 11 distinct entries while two classifier entries and three additional replacement entries coexist, the projected total would be 25 and that transition would not pass the check. Those counts are an arithmetic illustration, not data for this design.
Could we make that example fit just by declaring the three replacement slots reserved?

No. Reservation accounts for entries; it does not raise the numerical cap. With the illustrative total of 25 against a cap of 24, the transition as projected is over budget. A different proposal or actual coexistence pattern would have to be evaluated anew, but the plan does not choose one.
If coalescing still leaves an endpoint snapshot that fails the capacity check, what happens?

The plan does not authorize that transition in its failing form. It does not specify whether to coalesce differently, defer the work, or use another approach. We cannot infer from the plan that every oversized intent eventually becomes admissible.
Does passing this capacity check make the endpoint snapshot committed?

No. Reserving capacity and committing a routing configuration are different steps. This plan specifies coalescing into endpoint snapshots and reserving for a 2×-capped transition; it does not define a commit operation or say that passing the rule check alone commits a snapshot.
Will this plan also prove that every packet follows one committed configuration?

Not by itself. It addresses oversized intermediate configurations and switch-rule capacity. Per-packet consistency additionally depends on how packets select a committed configuration and how its rules remain available along their paths. A transition can fit within the capacity cap without establishing that packet-level property.
And does admission prove that updates complete after controller connectivity recovers?

No. It prevents proceeding with a projected over-budget transition, but says nothing about whether every failed proposal can be reworked or when work finishes after reconnection. Completion is a separate requirement not established by this capacity plan.

Coalesce oversized intents into proposed endpoint snapshots, then, before each transition, reserve per-switch capacity for both rule banks, classifiers, and transient replacements. Admit the transition only when their projected simultaneous occupancy stays within 2× max(initial, final) at every switch. The plan does not yet supply results, a universal feasibility argument, or packet-consistency and recovery-completion guarantees.
